label: like, as (similarity)
meaning_en: A particle that attaches to a noun and means “like N, as N is”. It makes a comparison of quality or manner, and in a few time-noun collocations it adds the sense of “without fail” or “very early”.
usage: It attaches directly to a noun, without a space: “얼음같이 차갑다”. The predicate is usually an adjective or a verb that describes what the noun is like. Do not mix it up with the adverb “같이” (together), which follows “N와/과” and takes a space. Fixed collocations: “매일같이” (every single day), “새벽같이” (at the crack of dawn), “철석같이 믿다” (to trust unshakably).

examples.en: That person is as kind-hearted as an angel.

examples.ko: 네 손이 얼음같이 차가워서 깜짝 놀랐어.
examples.en: Your hands are as cold as ice, so I was startled.
Minjun goes to the library every single day.

examples.ko: 지수는 새벽같이 일어나 출근 준비를 했다.
examples.en: Jisu got up at the crack of dawn and got ready for work.
The trip passed by like a dream.

compare.difference: In similes “같이” and “처럼” are near-synonyms and can usually replace each other. The time-noun collocations (“매일같이”, “새벽같이”) are the set phrases of “같이”.

pair.en: That person is as kind as an angel.
That person is as kind as an angel.

compare.difference: The adverb “같이” (together) is a different word from the particle: it follows “N와/과” and means “in company with”. The particle only compares.

pair.en: The teacher is as easy to be around as a friend.
I watched a movie together with my friend.

pitfalls.note: Attached to a noun, it means “like”, not “together with”. For “together”, use “N와/과 같이”.
pitfalls.en: I watched a movie together with my friend.

topik_tip: The time-noun phrases “매일같이” and “새벽같이” are worth knowing as units: they are adverbs meaning “every single day” and “at the crack of dawn”, not similes.

label: listing every item, “X and Y and all”
meaning_en: A particle that is repeated on each noun in a list, “N이고 N이고 (다)”, and says that all of them are included: “be it A or B, all of it”. The sentence usually ends with a summing-up word such as “다” or “모두”.
usage: After a noun ending in a consonant it is “이고” (“밥이고”, “서울이고”); after a vowel the “이” drops (“커피고”, “차고”). It goes on every item, including the last, and the main clause normally sums up with “다/모두/전부” or makes a sweeping statement. Typical collocations: “낮이고 밤이고” (day and night), “이고 저고” (this and that). It is a spoken, slightly emphatic way of listing.

examples.en: The rice, the bread, everything looks delicious.
Minjun did nothing but work, day and night.

examples.ko: 서울이고 부산이고 주말에는 어디나 사람이 많다.
examples.en: Be it Seoul or Busan, there are crowds everywhere on weekends.

examples.ko: 요즘은 영화고 드라마고 볼 시간이 없어요.
examples.en: These days I have no time to watch movies, dramas, or anything.

examples.ko: 한국어는 문법이고 어휘고 하나도 쉬운 게 없다.
examples.en: In Korean, neither grammar nor vocabulary is easy at all.

compare.difference: “N이고 N이고” lists the items and covers all of them. “N이든 N이든” says it makes no difference which one: any of them will do.

pair.en: I eat fruit, vegetables, everything well.
Fruit or vegetables, give me whichever.

compare.difference: “하고” and “와/과” are the plain “and”. “이고” is not a plain “and”: it needs the repeated pattern and a sweeping main clause.

pair.en: I bought apples, pears, the lot.
I bought apples and pears.

pitfalls.note: The particle goes on every item, including the last. With only the first item marked, the list breaks off.
pitfalls.en: I ate the rice, the bread, all of it.

pitfalls.note: It is not a plain “and”. A simple list of two things takes “하고” or “와/과”.
pitfalls.en: I bought apples, pears, the lot.

topik_tip: Look for the pair “N이고 N이고” followed by “다/모두”. It reads as “all of them, no matter which”, similar in effect to “N이든 N이든 다”.

label: as, according to
meaning_en: A particle meaning “as N, in line with N”: the action or state follows the noun exactly. It is also used with a noun to say that each thing goes its own way (“제멋대로”, “각자 마음대로”).
usage: It attaches to a noun without a space: “계획대로”, “예상대로”, “약속대로”, “법대로”, “말씀대로”. After a verb or adjective modifier the same word is a dependent noun and is written with a space (“말한 대로”, “본 대로”). Common collocations: “예상대로” (as expected), “마음대로” (as one pleases), “순서대로” (in order).

examples.en: Everything went as planned.
As expected, the result was not good.
As promised, lunch is on me today.
I did as the teacher said, and the problem got solved.
Please handle it according to the law.

compare.difference: “말씀대로” (noun) and “말씀하신 대로” (verb form) mean the same. The first attaches to the noun, the second is a modifier plus a spaced word.

pair.en: I will do as you say.
I will do as you said.

compare.difference: “법대로” is plain and direct. “법에 따라” is the more formal, document-like way of saying “in accordance with the law”.

pair.en: We will handle it according to the law.
We will handle it in accordance with the law.

pitfalls.note: After a verb it is a separate word: write a space. Only after a noun is it attached.
pitfalls.en: I did as I said.

topik_tip: Spacing is the usual test item: “N대로” is attached, but “-은/는 대로” after a verb or adjective is spaced.

label: from (a source or starting point)
meaning_en: A formal particle marking the source or origin of something: the person or place something comes from, the one who sends, gives or causes it. It translates as “from”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “로부터” (“친구로부터”, “서울로부터”); after any other consonant it is “으로부터” (“집으로부터”, “사람으로부터”). It marks givers and senders (“받다, 듣다, 배우다”), sources (“들어오다”), and what one is freed or protected from (“벗어나다, 보호하다, 자유롭다”). It is written and formal; speech prefers “한테서/에게서” for people and “에서” for places.

examples.en: Yesterday I received a letter from an old friend.
This system was brought in from Japan.
We came to receive subsidy money from the government.
We must protect children from danger.

examples.ko: 학교는 역으로부터 걸어서 오 분 거리에 있다.
examples.en: The school is a five-minute walk from the station.

compare.difference: For a person as the source, “에게서” is the everyday choice and “으로부터” the written, formal one. The meaning is the same.

pair.en: I received a present from a friend.
I received a present from a friend.

compare.difference: For a place as a starting point, “에서” is the everyday particle; “으로부터” sounds more formal and is also used for time and distance.

pair.en: It is five minutes from the station.
It is five minutes from the station.

pitfalls.note: A noun ending in ㄹ takes “로부터”, never “으로부터”.
pitfalls.en: A letter came from Seoul.

pitfalls.note: It marks the source or giver, not the one who receives. The recipient takes “에게”.
pitfalls.en: I gave a present to a friend.

topik_tip: In 읽기 passages “으로부터” is found with verbs of receiving and release: “받다, 듣다, 벗어나다, 보호하다”.

label: as much as (degree)
meaning_en: A particle that attaches to a noun and means “to the same degree as N”: it compares extent, amount or level. In a negative sentence it means “not as ... as N”.
usage: It attaches to a noun or pronoun without a space: “너만큼”, “작년만큼”, “기대만큼”. The predicate expresses a degree (an adjective such as “크다” or a verb like “좋아하다”). With a negative it says that N is the higher standard (“작년만큼 덥지 않다”). “만큼은” singles out one thing for emphasis: “이번만큼은” (this time, at least), “이것만큼은”. The dependent noun “-ㄴ/는 만큼” after a verb is spaced and is a different row.

examples.en: Minjun is as tall as Jisu.
This year is not as hot as last year.

examples.ko: 나만큼 너를 아끼는 사람은 없을 거야.
examples.en: No one cares for you as much as I do.
The exam result was not as good as expected.
This time, I will keep my promise for sure.

compare.difference: “만큼” compares degree, “처럼” compares manner or likeness. The minimal pair differs in what is being matched.

pair.en: I want to sing as well as you do.
I want to sing like you.

compare.difference: “만큼” says two things are equal; “보다” says one is more than the other.

pair.en: They run as fast as Jisu.
They run faster than Jisu.

pitfalls.note: “만큼” matches degree. For manner or resemblance, use “처럼”.
pitfalls.en: I want to fly like a bird.

pitfalls.note: After a verb form it is a separate word with a space; only a noun takes it attached.
pitfalls.en: You get as much as you put in effort.

topik_tip: “N만큼 + negative” (“not as ... as N”) and “이번만큼은” (this time, at least) are the two shapes to recognise in exams.

label: to/at a person (speech, reaction)
meaning_en: A colloquial particle that marks the person a speech act or a reaction is aimed at, like “에게/한테” but limited to verbs such as “말하다, 시키다, 웃다, 화내다, 욕하다”. Typical shape: “나보고 ...(으)라고 하다” (they told me to ...).
usage: It attaches to person nouns and pronouns (“나보고, 너보고, 민준이보고”) and is heard in speech and informal writing. It is almost always followed by a verb of saying, commanding or reacting, often with a quoted clause: “나보고 가라고 했다”. It is not used with verbs of giving or receiving: those need “에게/한테”. The set phrase “나보고 어쩌라고?” means “What do you want me to do?”. Do not confuse it with “보고” from the verb “보다”.

examples.ko: 엄마가 나보고 방 좀 치우라고 했다.
examples.en: Mom told me to clean my room.
The teacher told Minjun to stand up.
People say I am diligent.

examples.ko: 승규는 아무 이유 없이 나보고 화를 냈다.
examples.en: Seunggyu got angry at me for no reason.
What is everyone expecting me to do?

compare.difference: With speech verbs “보고” and “한테” mean the same, and “한테” is the neutral, safer form. “보고” is only spoken-style and only with some verbs.

pair.en: Minjun told me to go.
Minjun told me to go.

pitfalls.note: “보고” does not go with verbs of giving or receiving; those take “한테/에게”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a book.

topik_tip: In reading dialogues the shape “N보고 ...라고 하다” is the same as “N한테 ...라고 하다”: read it as “told N to ...”.

label: only, nothing but
meaning_en: A particle meaning “only N, nothing other than N”. It typically closes the sentence with “이다” (“너뿐이야”) or appears in “N뿐만 아니라” (not only N but also).
usage: It attaches to a noun without a space and then needs “이다” (“너뿐이다”), “뿐이 아니다” or “뿐(만) 아니라”. It does not combine freely with an ordinary verb: for “only eat bread” use “만” (“빵만 먹었다”). After a verb modifier “뿐” is a dependent noun and is spaced (“웃을 뿐이다”, I can only laugh). Common phrases: “하나뿐” (the only one), “뿐만 아니라” (not only ... but also).

examples.en: You are the only one I can trust.
There was nothing in the room but one old chair.

examples.ko: 그 가수는 노래뿐만 아니라 춤도 잘 춘다.
examples.en: Besides singing, that singer also dances well.

examples.ko: 이 일을 할 수 있는 사람은 지수뿐입니다.
examples.en: Jisu is the only person who can do this job.
All that remains is regret.

compare.difference: “만” attaches to any word and works with any predicate. “뿐” closes the sentence with “이다” and sounds more final.

pair.en: I trust only you.
The only person I trust is you.

compare.difference: “뿐이다” and “밖에 없다” are near-synonyms for “nothing but”. “뿐” ends in “이다”, “밖에” always needs a negative.

pair.en: You are the only one I can trust.
There is no one I can trust but you.

pitfalls.note: With an ordinary verb the particle for “only” is “만”; “뿐” needs “이다” or “뿐 아니라”.
pitfalls.en: I ate only bread.

pitfalls.note: After a verb form it is spaced as a dependent noun.
pitfalls.en: All I could do was laugh.

topik_tip: “뿐만 아니라 ... 도” is the standard “not only ... but also” frame in 읽기.

label: calling a person (vocative)
meaning_en: The vocative particle “아/야” attached to a name or a noun when calling or addressing someone close or younger: “민준아, 이리 와.”
usage: After a consonant-final name it is “아” (“민준아, 유민아, 지영아”), after a vowel-final name “야” (“지수야, 승규야, 영수야”). It is used to friends, younger people, children and also to animals and things in poems and songs (“달아”). It is intimate speech (“해체” or “해라체” sentences follow it) and is not used to someone you must show respect to: with elders you use the title alone (“선생님, ...”) and with polite adults “씨”. Common: “얘들아” (hey, kids).

examples.en: Minjun, have you eaten?
Jisu, come over here for a moment.
Yumin, what time is the exam tomorrow?
Seunggyu, it has been a while. Have you been well?
Kids, be quiet.
Moon, you are shining bright again today.

compare.difference: “아/야” is for close friends and juniors; “씨” is the neutral, polite way to address an adult you are not close to.

pair.en: Jisu, where are you going?
Jisu, where are you going?

pitfalls.note: After a consonant-final name the particle is “아”, not “야”.
pitfalls.en: Minjun, come here.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel-final name it is “야”, not “아”.
pitfalls.en: Jisu, what are you doing?

topik_tip: Pick the form from the last sound of the name: consonant gives “아”, vowel gives “야”.

label: polite “요” on words and phrases
meaning_en: A particle that adds politeness to a word, phrase or clause ending, turning intimate speech (“해체”) into the soft polite “해요체”: “저기요”, “빨리요”, “그래서요?”.
usage: It attaches to nouns, adverbs and the ends of clauses, whether or not a full ending follows (“물 좀요”, “지금 바로요?”, “그런데요”, “그래서요?”). That is why it appears on fragments and in the middle of sentences: “저는요, 어제요, ...”. In conversation “여기요” and “저기요” are the standard ways to call a waiter or stranger. It does not stack onto “합쇼체” endings (“-습니다”).

examples.en: Excuse me, could we get some water here?
As for me, I am going to the library.
And then? What happened next?

examples.ko: 지금 바로요? 아직 준비가 안 됐는데요.
examples.en: Right now? I am not ready yet.
Two coffees here, please.

compare.difference: The particle “요” gives soft, conversational politeness (“해요체”); “-습니다” is the formal “합쇼체” used in speeches, announcements and business.

pair.en: Are you going now?
Are you going now?

pitfalls.note: Do not add “요” to a “합쇼체” ending. Choose the “해요체” ending instead.
pitfalls.en: Thank you.

pitfalls.note: A bare noun with “요” works as an answer fragment, but a full statement needs the copula “이에요”.
pitfalls.en: I am a student.

topik_tip: In listening items, “요” on a fragment or after a pause marks “해요체” speech: it is polite, not a different meaning.

label: quoting directly, “called ...”
meaning_en: A quotation particle: “라고” follows a directly quoted word or sentence, and “이라고” follows a consonant-final noun being named or quoted. “N(이)라고 하다” means “to be called N”.
usage: In a direct quote it attaches to the quoted words (“‘가자’라고 말했다”). With a noun it is “이라고” after a consonant (“한글이라고”) and “라고” after a vowel (“김치라고”). It combines with “하다, 말하다, 부르다, 외치다, 소리치다, 쓰다”. The collocation “(이)라고 해서” means “just because it is ...”. For indirect quotes the endings “-다고/-라고” are used instead.

examples.en: In Korean this food is called “비빔밥”.
The teacher said, “Hand in your homework by tomorrow.”
My friend calls me a “genius”.
The child came running, shouting “Mom!”

examples.ko: 부자라고 해서 다 행복한 것은 아니다.
examples.en: Just because people are rich does not mean they are all happy.

compare.difference: “라고” repeats the words as spoken (direct quote). “-다고” reports them from the speaker’s own point of view (indirect quote), so the sentence form changes.

pair.en: I said, “I'm hungry.”
I said that I was hungry.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel-final noun there is no “이”: it is “라고”.
pitfalls.en: This is called kimchi.

pitfalls.note: After a consonant-final noun “이” is needed.
pitfalls.en: This letter system is called “한글”.

topik_tip: Telling direct (“라고”) from indirect (“-다고”) quotation is a typical grammar question; in direct quotes the quoted words stay unchanged.

label: past cut off from the present
meaning_en: A doubled past marker that presents an event or state as finished and no longer connected to the present: “I used to ...”, “there was a time when ...”. It often hints that the situation has since changed.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and to “이다”: “가다 → 갔었다”, “먹다 → 먹었었다”, “살다 → 살았었다”, “하다 → 했었다”. It sets the situation apart from now, so it pairs with time words such as “예전에, 전에, 어릴 때, 한때, 그때”, and it is often followed by a contrast with the present (“-었었는데 지금은 ...”). If a result still holds, or the event is recent, plain “-었-” is used. In speech it is common with “-었었어요” in the “해요체”.

examples.en: I used to live in the countryside when I was little.
I used to smoke, but I have quit now.

examples.ko: 그 가게는 전에 여기에 있었었는데 이사 갔나 봐요.
examples.en: That shop used to be here, but it seems to have moved.
I, too, played the guitar for a while once.
This road used to be very narrow.

compare.difference: Plain “-었-” just reports a past event. “-었었-” adds that it is over and no longer true now.

pair.en: I lived in Seoul last year.
I used to live in Seoul last year.

compare.difference: “-은 적이 있다” says one has had the experience. “-었었-” says the event happened in the past and is over, without focusing on experience.

pair.en: I have been to Jeju Island.
I went to Jeju Island.

pitfalls.note: It marks a situation that is no longer true, so it does not fit a state that continues now.
pitfalls.right: 저는 어릴 때 이 동네에 살았었어요.
pitfalls.en: I used to live in this neighborhood when I was little.

topik_tip: In reading passages, “-었었-” plus “지금은” signals a contrast between a past situation and the present.

label: if, once (condition)
meaning_en: A connective ending meaning “if it is the case that ...” or “once it turns out that ...”. It sets a condition that may come true, and the main clause is normally a command, request, suggestion or promise.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems: “도착하다 → 도착하거든”, “좋다 → 좋거든”, “학생이다 → 학생이거든”; it can follow “-었-” (“끝났거든”). The main clause is an order, request or invitation (“-아라/-세요/-자”) or a promise, rarely a plain statement of fact: for “비가 오면 길이 막힌다” use “-으면”. The sentence-final “-거든(요)” (giving a reason) is a different row, “-거든2”.

examples.en: Call me when you get home.
Once the exam date is set, let's study together.
If a word you do not know comes up, look it up in a dictionary.
If you like it, take it.
If it is hard, tell me at any time.

compare.difference: With a command or a proposal as the main clause the two are near-synonyms. “-으면” also handles plain statements, habits and general truths; “-거든” does not.

pair.en: Once the rain stops, let's set off.
When the rain stops, the roads get jammed.

compare.difference: “-거든2” closes a sentence and gives a reason (“I'm hungry, I skipped breakfast, see”). “-거든1” is a conditional that continues into a main clause.

pair.en: If you are hungry, eat first.
I'm hungry. I did not eat breakfast, you see.

pitfalls.note: The main clause needs to be a command, request, suggestion or promise, not a statement of fact.
pitfalls.en: If it rains, use an umbrella.

topik_tip: “-거든” followed by an imperative (“-아라/-세요”) or “-자” is the condition ending; when the clause closes the sentence, it is “-거든2”.

label: listing examples, “things like X or Y”
meaning_en: A connective ending that lists actions or states as examples, usually followed by “하다”: “X도 한다거나 Y도 한다거나 하다” means “do things like X or Y”. It is a contraction of “-는다고 하거나”.
usage: Verbs take “-ㄴ다거나/-는다거나” (“가다 → 간다거나”, “먹다 → 먹는다거나”, “놀다 → 논다거나”, “보다 → 본다거나”); adjectives take “-다거나” (“피곤하다거나”); nouns take “-(이)라거나” (“학생이라거나”); commands and suggestions take “-(으)라거나, -자거나”. It is normally repeated at least twice, and the example list ends with “하다” or a sweeping noun such as “일”. It is conversational and a little vague on purpose.

examples.ko: 주말에는 영화를 본다거나 산책을 한다거나 해요.
examples.en: On weekends I do things like watching a movie or going for a walk.

examples.ko: 민준이는 피곤하다거나 힘들다거나 하는 말을 절대 하지 않는다.
examples.en: Minjun never says things like being tired or finding things hard.

examples.ko: 비가 온다거나 눈이 온다거나 해도 약속은 지켜야 한다.
examples.en: Even if it rains or snows or something, a promise has to be kept.

examples.ko: 스트레스를 받을 때는 음악을 듣는다거나 운동을 한다거나 하면 도움이 된다.
examples.en: When you are stressed, things like listening to music or exercising help.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 학생이라거나 직장인이라거나 하는 정보는 없었다.
examples.en: There was no information such as whether that person was a student or an office worker.

compare.difference: “-거나” offers two alternatives (“A or B”). “-는다거나 ... 하다” gives examples among others, so the list is open.

pair.en: I read a book or watch a movie.
I do things like reading or watching movies.

compare.difference: “-기도 하고 ... -기도 하다” is a close alternative that says the speaker does each of these things as well. The two are near-synonyms.

pair.ko: 책을 읽기도 하고 영화를 보기도 해요.
pair.en: I read books and also watch movies.
I do things like reading or watching movies.

pitfalls.note: The present of an action verb ending in a vowel takes “-ㄴ다거나”, not “-는다거나”.
pitfalls.en: I do things like watching a movie or reading a book.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㄹ drops it before “-ㄴ다거나”.
pitfalls.en: I do things like hanging out with friends or watching movies.

topik_tip: Pick the form from the stem: vowel gives “-ㄴ다거나”, consonant gives “-는다거나”, ㄹ drops (“논다거나”); adjectives are “-다거나”.

label: doing X, with a side result (reason)
meaning_en: A connective ending for a reason or cause that is an action someone is doing or a state someone claims: “because they were doing X, (an unwelcome or surprising) Y”. It often has the feel of “in the course of trying to X” or “on the pretext of X”.
usage: Verbs take “-ㄴ다고/-는다고” (“잡다 → 잡는다고”, “하다 → 한다고”, “빼다 → 뺀다고”, “만들다 → 만든다고”), adjectives “-다고” (“바쁘다고”), nouns “-(이)라고”. The subjects of the two clauses can differ. The main clause is often something undesirable or unexpected. In everyday speech the collocation “-ㄴ다고 난리다” (making a fuss about doing X) is common. It differs from the quoting “-는다고3”.

examples.en: I sprayed insecticide in an attempt to catch the cockroach.

examples.ko: 민준이가 책을 읽는다고 밤새 불을 켜 놓았어요.
examples.en: Minjun kept the light on all night on account of reading a book.

examples.ko: 동생이 요리를 한다고 부엌을 엉망으로 만들었다.
examples.en: My younger sibling made a mess of the kitchen trying to cook.
Jisu does not even get in touch, claiming to be busy.
These days everyone is making a fuss about losing weight.

compare.difference: “-느라고” takes verbs only and needs the same subject in both clauses. “-는다고” also allows adjectives and a different subject, and often hints that the effort did not pay off.

pair.en: My younger sibling made the kitchen messy trying to cook.
My younger sibling made the kitchen messy because of cooking.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-다고”, never “-ㄴ다고”.
pitfalls.en: Minjun does not even get in touch, claiming to be busy.

topik_tip: Do not translate it as a plain “because”: it describes someone doing or claiming something, and the result is usually a pity or a surprise.

label: but, although (formal)
meaning_en: A formal, mostly written connective ending meaning “but, although”: the second clause contrasts with the first. In the repeated pattern “-으나 -으나” it means “whether ... or ...”.
usage: After a stem ending in a vowel or ㄹ it is “-나”, after other consonants “-으나”. Real stems: “가다 → 가나”, “작다 → 작으나”, “살다 → 사나” (the ㄹ drops), “어렵다 → 어려우나” (ㅂ-irregular), “덥다 → 더우나”, “노력했다 → 노력했으나”; with “이다” it is “이나”. It belongs to news, essays and formal speeches; everyday speech uses “-지만”. The pattern “비가 오나 눈이 오나” means “rain or snow, regardless”.

examples.ko: 민준이는 열심히 노력했으나 결과는 좋지 않았다.
examples.en: Minjun worked hard, but the result was not good.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 어려우나 풀 수 없는 것은 아니다.
examples.en: This problem is difficult, but it is not unsolvable.
The price is high, but the quality is reliable.
On the outside it looks calm, but inside it is uneasy.

examples.ko: 비가 오나 눈이 오나 민준이는 매일 아침 달린다.
examples.en: Rain or snow, Minjun runs every morning.

compare.difference: “-지만” is the everyday form and also fine in writing; “-으나” is formal and mostly written. The meaning is the same.

pair.en: I worked hard, but I failed.
I worked hard, but I failed.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㄹ drops the ㄹ before “-나”.
pitfalls.en: They live in poverty, but their hearts are rich.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우” before the vowel.
pitfalls.wrong: 이 문제는 어렵으나 풀 수 있다.
pitfalls.right: 이 문제는 어려우나 풀 수 있다.
pitfalls.en: This problem is hard, but it can be solved.

topik_tip: “-으나” and “-지만” share a meaning; the register is what tells them apart.

label: because I was busy doing (same subject)
meaning_en: A connective ending for a cause that is the speaker's (or subject's) own activity: “because I was busy doing X, Y (usually a bad result)”. The first action takes up time and energy and that is why the second could not happen.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only, never after “-었-” or “-겠-”. The subject of both clauses must be the same, and the main clause is a statement or question, not a command or suggestion (“공부하느라고 가지 마세요” is wrong). Real stems: “하다 → 하느라고”, “놀다 → 노느라고” (the ㄹ drops), “만들다 → 만드느라고”, “걷다 → 걷느라고”. The main clause is typically negative or about hardship: “못 했다, 늦었다, 바쁘다, 고생하다, 정신이 없다”. A short form “-느라” exists.

examples.en: I could not sleep last night because I was doing homework.
I was in a frenzy looking after the child.

examples.ko: 시험 준비를 하느라고 친구도 못 만났어.
examples.en: I was so busy preparing for the exam that I could not even meet friends.

examples.ko: 영화를 보느라고 전화 온 줄도 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I was watching a movie, so I did not even know a call had come.
I had a hard time writing the report all night.

compare.difference: “-느라고” describes an activity the subject chose to do; “-는 바람에” fits an event that was not planned. Both can be used with a verb, and the translation can look the same.

pair.en: I missed the bus because I was talking with a friend.
I missed the bus because I got to talking with a friend.

compare.difference: “-어서” works for any cause and any subject. “-느라고” is limited to one's own busy activity.

pair.en: I could not sleep because I was doing homework.
I could not sleep because I had a lot of homework.

pitfalls.note: It cannot take a tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I could not sleep because I was doing homework.

pitfalls.note: Both clauses need the same subject; with a different subject use “-는 바람에”.
pitfalls.wrong: 민준이가 노래하느라고 내가 잠을 못 잤다.
pitfalls.right: 민준이가 노래하는 바람에 내가 잠을 못 잤다.
pitfalls.en: Minjun sang, and so I could not sleep.

topik_tip: Same subject, verb stem, no tense ending, negative result: that checklist covers most “-느라고” questions.

label: so that, until, to the point that
meaning_en: A connective ending with three overlapping uses: a purpose (“so that, in order that”), a limit (“until, to the point that”) and a degree. In “-도록 하다” it means “make sure to, see to it that”.
usage: It attaches directly to verb or adjective stems and does not take a tense ending: “크게 말하도록”. The ㄹ stays before ㄷ: “살다 → 살도록”, “만들다 → 만들도록”. As a purpose it is formal and close to “-게”: “들을 수 있도록”, “늦지 않도록”. As a limit it points to the extent: “목이 쉬도록” (until hoarse), “밤새도록” (all night long), “해가 지도록”. Also: “되도록 빨리” (as soon as possible).

examples.ko: 모두가 들을 수 있도록 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so that everyone can hear.
Minjun sang until hoarse.
It snowed all through the night.

examples.ko: 약속 시간에 늦지 않도록 일찍 출발했다.
examples.en: I set off early so that I would not be late for the appointment.

examples.ko: 회의 시간에는 휴대전화를 꺼 두도록 하세요.
examples.en: Please make sure to turn off your phones during the meeting.

compare.difference: In the purpose use “-도록” and “-게” are near-synonyms; “-도록” is a little more formal. Only “-도록” has the “until / to the point that” use.

pair.en: I spoke loudly so that it could be heard well.
I spoke loudly so that it could be heard well.

compare.difference: “-도록 하다” and “-게 하다” overlap when someone is made to do something. “-도록 하세요” is the polite “please make sure to ...”.

pair.en: Please make sure the child goes to bed early.
Please have the child go to bed early.

pitfalls.note: The “until” use does not take a past tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I sang until my voice went hoarse.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-도록”.
pitfalls.wrong: 누구나 쉽게 만드도록 레시피를 단순하게 했다.
pitfalls.right: 누구나 쉽게 만들도록 레시피를 단순하게 했다.
pitfalls.en: I kept the recipe simple so that anyone could make it easily.

topik_tip: In 읽기 answers, “-도록” is “so that” when a goal follows and “until/to the point that” when a result or extreme follows; the two choices are usually clear from the main clause.

label: doing X and taking it along (then Y)
meaning_en: A connective ending for “do X to an object and carry it somewhere, then do Y with it”: the object of the first action is brought to another place. “빵을 사다가 먹다” is “buy bread and bring it to eat it (elsewhere)”.
usage: It attaches to transitive verb stems with the usual “-아/어” vowel (“사다가”, “가져다가”, “빌려다가”, “데려다가”), and the verb after it takes the same object and often a destination. Stems ending in ㅡ drop it (“담그다 → 담가다가”). It contracts to “-어다”: “사다 주다”, “데려다 주다”. Typical: “사다가 주다, 가져다가 놓다, 빌려다가 읽다”. The ending “-다가” alone (interruption) is a different pattern.

examples.ko: 마트에서 우유를 사다가 냉장고에 넣어 두었다.
examples.en: I picked up milk at the supermarket and put it in the fridge.

examples.ko: 친구가 우리 집에 선물을 가져다가 놓고 갔다.
examples.en: My friend brought a present to our house, left it there and went off.

examples.ko: 승규는 나를 집 앞까지 데려다 줬다.
examples.en: Seunggyu took me as far as my doorstep.
I got some kimchi from the neighbors and brought it home to eat.
I picked up the tissue on the floor and threw it in the trash can.
I packed up some side dishes and took them over to share with the neighbors.

compare.difference: “-어서” only says one action follows the other. “-어다가” adds that the object is carried to another place.

pair.en: I bought bread and brought it over to eat.
I bought bread and ate it.

compare.difference: “사다가 주다” and “사 가지고 와서 주다” are near-synonyms. “-어 가지고” is the more spoken form.

pair.en: I bought bread and brought it to give.
I bought bread, came with it and gave it.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㅡ drops it before the vowel: “담그다” becomes “담가”.
pitfalls.en: I made kimchi and took it over to share.

topik_tip: Moving the object is the key: “-어다가” needs an object that travels, as in “사다가, 가져다가, 데려다가”.

label: even if, even though
meaning_en: A concessive connective ending: “even if X, ... / no matter how X, ...”. The first clause does not stop the second from being true, and X may be hypothetical or a fact.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems with the “-아/어” vowel: “오다 → 와도”, “먹다 → 먹어도”, “하다 → 해도”, “쓰다 → 써도”, “듣다 → 들어도” (ㄷ becomes ㄹ), “어렵다 → 어려워도”, “빠르다 → 빨라도”; “학생이다 → 학생이어도”. Often with “아무리” (however much), “-어도 -어도” (no matter how much), and negative or contrasting main clauses. It is not the permission pattern “-어도 되다”.

examples.en: Even if it rains, we will set off as planned.

examples.ko: 아무리 바빠도 밥은 챙겨 먹어야 해요.
examples.en: However busy you are, you have to make sure to eat.

examples.ko: 어려워도 포기하지 말고 끝까지 해 보자.
examples.en: Even if it is hard, let's not give up and try to the end.

examples.ko: 열 번을 들어도 무슨 뜻인지 모르겠어요.
examples.en: Even after hearing it ten times, I do not understand what it means.
No matter how much I eat, I am still hungry.

compare.difference: “-어도” grants a hypothetical or general case (“even if”); “-지만” states a factual contrast (“but”).

pair.en: I will go even if it rains.
It is raining, but I am going.

compare.difference: “-더라도” is a near-synonym that stresses a hypothetical assumption and is a little more formal. Most sentences with “-어도” can use it.

pair.en: It is fine even if you fail.
It is fine even if you fail.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular stem changes ㄷ to ㄹ before a vowel.
pitfalls.en: No matter how much I listen, I do not understand.

pitfalls.note: After a noun the copula is “이어도” (“여도” after a vowel), not “이도”.
pitfalls.en: Even a student has to keep good manners.

topik_tip: Do not mix it up with the permission pattern “-어도 되다”; when no “되다” follows, “-어도” is “even if”.

label: only if, must (necessary condition)
meaning_en: A connective ending that makes the first clause an essential condition: “only if X can Y”, “Y is possible only when X”. In “-어야 소용없다/-어 봐야” it also means “even if, however much”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems with the “-아/어” vowel: “공부하다 → 공부해야”, “오다 → 와야”, “듣다 → 들어야”, “쉽다 → 쉬워야”, “싸다 → 싸야”; “학생이다 → 학생이어야”. The main clause is usually a present or future judgment (“-ㄹ 수 있다, 되다, 하다”). The emphatic form “-어야만” is a near-synonym. “후회해야 소용없다” means “regretting is useless”.

examples.ko: 열심히 공부해야 시험에 합격할 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only if you study hard can you pass the exam.

examples.ko: 직접 먹어 봐야 맛을 알 수 있다.
examples.en: You can only know the taste by trying it yourself.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋아야 소풍을 갈 수 있어요.
examples.en: We can go on a picnic only if the weather is good.
Regretting at this point is no use.
Only if the cost is low will many people use it.

compare.difference: “-으면” says X is enough for Y; “-어야” says X is required for Y.

pair.en: If you study, you pass.
Only if you study do you pass.

compare.difference: “-어야만” is the same pattern with “만” added for emphasis; the meaning is the same and the tone firmer.

pair.en: It improves only with practice.
It improves only with practice.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우” and adds “-어”: “쉽다” becomes “쉬워”.
pitfalls.en: Only if the problem is easy can they solve it.

topik_tip: Contrast “-으면” (sufficient) and “-어야” (necessary): the second says “only if”.
